Last year, I made a decision that changed how I lead my team: I stopped scheduling status meetings.

At first, I was nervous. Status meetings felt like the glue that held everything together. But after reviewing our calendars, I realized my team of twelve was spending nearly eight hours a week in meetings that mostly repeated information already available in our project tracker.

Here is what we did instead:

1. We moved updates to a shared written format every Monday morning.
2. We reserved live meetings only for decisions, not updates.
3. We made every meeting optional unless someone had a specific decision to make.

The results surprised me. Project delivery times improved by 18 percent. Team satisfaction scores rose. And perhaps most importantly, people reported feeling trusted.

The lesson? Meetings are a tool, not a ritual. If a meeting does not lead to a decision or a better relationship, it probably should be an email.

What is one recurring meeting you could eliminate this week?

#Leadership #Productivity #FutureOfWork

I failed my first technical interview. Badly.

Ten years ago, I sat in a conference room, stared at a whiteboard, and completely froze on a basic array problem. I walked out convinced I was not cut out for software engineering.

Today, I lead a team of fifteen engineers at a fast-growing fintech company.

What changed? Three things:

First, I stopped treating failure as a verdict and started treating it as data. Every rejection told me exactly what to practice next.

Second, I found a mentor who reminded me that nobody writes perfect code on a whiteboard under pressure.

Third, I kept showing up. Consistency beats talent more often than we admit.

If you are early in your career and feeling discouraged, remember this: the people you admire have all failed publicly at some point. The difference is that they kept going.

Your setback is not the end of your story. It might be the opening chapter.

Agree? Share this with someone who needs encouragement today.

Three lessons from analyzing 500 customer churn interviews:

1. Customers rarely leave because of price alone. In 71 percent of cases, price was mentioned alongside a lack of perceived value. When customers do not understand how a product helps them, any price feels too high.

2. The first 30 days matter most. Customers who reached a meaningful outcome within their first month were four times more likely to renew.

3. Silence is the biggest warning sign. Accounts that stopped logging in for two weeks churned at triple the average rate, yet most teams were not monitoring usage drops.

The takeaway for SaaS leaders: invest in onboarding, track engagement proactively, and make your value visible at every touchpoint.

Retention is not a department. It is a company-wide discipline.

What patterns have you noticed in your own churn data? I would love to hear your thoughts in the comments.

Sustainability reporting is no longer optional for mid-sized manufacturers, and the regulatory landscape is shifting quickly.

With new disclosure requirements arriving in the next two years, many operations leaders are asking the same question: where do we start?

Based on my work with over thirty facilities, here is a simple starting framework:

Measure first. You cannot reduce what you have not quantified. Begin with energy, water, and waste data across your largest sites.

Prioritize by impact. Focus on the three categories that account for the majority of your emissions rather than trying to solve everything at once.

Build a narrative. Investors and customers want to understand not just your numbers, but your plan for improving them.

Progress beats perfection. Companies that begin reporting early gain a significant advantage in both compliance readiness and brand trust.

Where is your organization on the sustainability journey? Let me know below.

Spent my saturday fixing a bug that turned out to be a trailing space in a config file. Four hours. FOUR.

The symptom was weird too. Our staging deploy worked, prod didn't, and the logs just said 'connection refused' which tells you absolutely nothing. I rewrote the retry logic. I blamed DNS. I blamed the load balancer, and then I blamed myself, in that order.

Then my coworker Anita glanced at my screen over zoom and went 'is that a space after the hostname?' It was.

I used to think seniority meant not making these mistakes. Now I think it means you've made enough of them that you start diffing the boring stuff first. Whitespace, env vars, timezones. Check those before you touch any code.

Anyway, we added a lint step for config files on Monday. Took twenty minutes. Should've done it two years ago.

Hot take that'll probably annoy some recruiters: I've stopped reading cover letters.

Not because they're bad. Some are lovely. But after hiring for our ops team three times I noticed the people I actually hired never had a great cover letter. What they had was a weird little detail on the resume. One guy ran a bike repair co-op. One woman listed 'moved 4 times in 3 years, learned to pack a truck fast.' I remembered both of them a month later.

So now I skim for the odd detail, then I call. 15 minutes, no script, I just ask what they were doing the last time they lost track of time at work.

It's not scientific, my sample is like nine people. But our first-year turnover dropped and I'm sticking with it until someone shows me it's luck.

Anyone else hiring this way, or am I just being lazy?

Teaching 8th grade math for 14 years has taught me one thing that I wish more ed-tech founders understood: kids don't hate math, they hate being wrong in front of people.

I've watched a student who's clearly got the answer in her head refuse to say it out loud because last week she got called out. I've had a kid erase a correct solution because the guy next to him wrote something different.

So my best tools aren't flashy. Mini whiteboards, where everybody holds up an answer at the same time. Anonymous warm-ups. Letting the 'wrong' answer be the day's discussion, with no names attached.

Getting Started with DataBridge

DataBridge is a lightweight Python library for moving data between relational databases and cloud storage. This section walks you through installation and your first transfer.

Installation

DataBridge requires Python 3.9 or later. Install it from PyPI using pip:

pip install databridge

To verify the installation, run databridge --version. You should see the current version number printed to the terminal.

Configuring a connection

Before transferring data, you need to define a source and a destination. Create a file named bridge.yaml in your project directory and specify the connection details for each. Credentials should be provided through environment variables rather than stored directly in the file. DataBridge reads variables prefixed with DB_ by default.

Running your first transfer

Once configured, run databridge sync to begin. The tool will validate both connections, estimate the volume of data, and then transfer tables in parallel. A progress summary is displayed on completion, including row counts and any skipped records. If a transfer fails, DataBridge automatically retries up to three times before reporting an error.

Authentication

The Orbit API uses bearer tokens to authenticate requests. Every request to a protected endpoint must include an Authorization header containing a valid access token.

Obtaining a token

To obtain an access token, send a POST request to the /v1/auth/token endpoint with your client ID and client secret in the request body. A successful response returns a JSON object containing the access token, its type, and an expiration time in seconds. Access tokens are valid for one hour.

Using a token

Include the token in the Authorization header using the Bearer scheme, for example: Authorization: Bearer YOUR_ACCESS_TOKEN. Requests without a valid token will receive a 401 Unauthorized response.

Refreshing a token

When a token expires, request a new one using the refresh token returned with your initial response. Refresh tokens are valid for 30 days. Store them securely and never expose them in client-side code.

Best practices

Rotate your client secrets regularly, restrict token scopes to the minimum required, and always make API requests over HTTPS.

How to Set Up Two-Factor Authentication

Two-factor authentication adds an extra layer of protection to your account by requiring a second form of verification when you sign in. Follow the steps below to enable it.

Step 1: Open your account settings. Click your profile picture in the top-right corner and select Settings, then choose the Security tab.

Step 2: Locate the Two-Factor Authentication section and click Enable. You will be asked to confirm your password.

Step 3: Choose your verification method. You can use an authenticator app, such as Google Authenticator or Authy, or receive codes by text message. We recommend an authenticator app for better security.

Step 4: Scan the QR code displayed on screen with your authenticator app, then enter the six-digit code the app generates.

Step 5: Save your recovery codes. These one-time codes allow you to access your account if you lose your device. Store them in a secure location, such as a password manager.

Once complete, you will be prompted for a verification code each time you sign in from a new device.

Heads up before you run the migration script: it will wipe the staging table. I found this out the hard way, so I'm writing it here.

The script lives in scripts/migrate_users.py. What it does, in order: it connects to whatever database DATABASE_URL points at, drops and recreates the users_staging table, then copies rows over from the legacy users table, skipping anything with a null email. About 3% of our old rows fall in that bucket, so don't panic if the counts don't match.

To run it locally:

1. Copy .env.example to .env and set DATABASE_URL to your local postgres. Please do not point it at the shared dev database.
2. Run python scripts/migrate_users.py --dry-run first. It prints what it would do and touches nothing.
3. If the numbers look sane, drop the flag.

It takes around 40 seconds for 200k rows on my laptop. If it hangs on the copy step, it's almost always a stale connection, just kill it and rerun, it's safe to repeat.

Rate limits, the short version.

The API allows 100 requests per minute per key. Go over and you get a 429 with a Retry-After header telling you how many seconds to wait. Please actually read that header instead of retrying in a tight loop, because we'll temporarily block keys that hammer us, and unblocking takes a support ticket.

A few things that aren't obvious. Batch endpoints (anything ending in /bulk) count as one request no matter how many items you send, up to 500 items. The /search endpoint is heavier and counts as five. Webhook deliveries to you don't count against anything.

If you need more headroom, say you're doing a big backfill, email us before you start and we'll bump your limit for a day or two. We've said yes every time so far.

Tip: cache GET /products. It changes maybe once a day, and most people we've seen polling it every few seconds don't need to be.

Troubleshooting: the build fails with 'module not found'

This one catches a lot of people, so here's what's usually going on.

Nine times out of ten, it's a stale node_modules folder after switching branches. Delete it, delete package-lock.json only if you've been fiddling with versions (otherwise leave it alone), and run npm ci. Not npm install, ci, since it respects the lockfile exactly.

If that doesn't fix it, check your Node version with node -v. We need 20 or higher. If you're on 18 you'll get the error above for the ESM-only packages, and the message really doesn't point you at the actual cause. We know, it's on the list.

Still stuck? Look at the import path. Our linter doesn't catch wrong casing, and macOS doesn't care about it but the CI box (Linux) very much does. So Utils.ts versus utils.ts can pass locally and fail in the pipeline. Yes, that cost somebody a whole afternoon.

If none of this works, open an issue and paste your full error, not just the last line.

Configuring environment variables

The app reads its settings from environment variables at startup, which keeps secrets out of the codebase and makes it easy to run the same build in different places. Here is how each one behaves.

PORT sets the port the server listens on. It defaults to 3000, and in most hosted environments the platform sets it for you, so you usually do not need to touch it.

LOG_LEVEL controls how chatty the logs are. Valid values are debug, info, warn and error. In production we run at info; debug is useful on your laptop but will fill up a disk fast under real traffic.

SESSION_SECRET is required. The server refuses to boot without it, on purpose, rather than falling back to some default value. Generate a long random string, for example with openssl rand -hex 32, and keep it the same across all instances, otherwise users will be logged out whenever the load balancer sends them to a different server.

Finally, CACHE_TTL is the number of seconds responses stay cached, default 60. Set it to 0 to turn caching off while you are debugging.

Shipping a Series B rollout doesn't have to feel like a fire drill. After our first ten engineering hires, I learned that the hardest part was never the code itself. It was getting people to agree on what done meant before they started.

So we wrote one page. It lists the three things a feature must do before it leaves a branch, who signs off, and what gets rolled back if it breaks at 2am. It took an afternoon and saved us weeks of argument later.

I'd push other founders to do the same. Keep it short. Revisit it once a quarter. If nobody can explain your definition of done in one sentence, that's the real problem to fix.

What's the most useful engineering norm your team has written down? I'd genuinely like to borrow a few.

We launched a feature last spring that I was sure would change everything. Two weeks in, almost nobody was using it. I spent a bad weekend reading support tickets and realized we had built a solution to a problem people had stopped having.

Here's the embarrassing part. The signal was there months earlier. A customer had mentioned, almost in passing, that they'd stopped doing the thing we were automating. I wrote it down and then ignored it because I was excited about the roadmap.

I'm not writing this to beat myself up. I'm writing it because a lot of us are building right now, and the loud feature requests are not always the honest ones. Go talk to the quiet customers. Ask them what they stopped doing.

Anyone else have a launch that taught them more about listening than about shipping?

Meetings. I said it. I've been in a lot of them this month and I'm starting to think half of them exist because someone needed a calendar slot to feel productive.

Patient data privacy is not a checkbox. For healthtech teams, it shapes how you design every integration, every analytics pipeline, and every support workflow.

Three practices have made the biggest difference for our product team this year. First, we minimize what we collect: if a field is not needed for the clinical task, it does not enter the system. Second, we separate identifiers from clinical records so a breach of one store does not expose the other. Third, we review every third-party SDK before it touches a production screen.

None of these ideas are new. What's new is how quickly a small change, like a session replay tool added for debugging, can create exposure that nobody intended.

I spent eleven years as a charge nurse before I moved into product. People keep asking if the switch was hard. Honestly, the hardest part was learning to stop fixing things myself.

Supply chains broke in public over the last few years, and most companies responded by buying more safety stock. That helped for a while. It also tied up cash and hid the real fragility.

The more useful response is mapping. Know not just your tier-one suppliers but the two or three layers below them, especially for components where one plant makes most of the world's supply. Then ask a plain question: if this site stopped for six weeks, what would we do on Monday?

We found three single points of failure this way, none of which appeared on any procurement dashboard. Two were fixed with a second qualified supplier. One we simply accepted and built a contingency for.

Resilience is not about eliminating risk. It's about knowing where the weak joints are before someone else finds them for you.

## Installation

Install the CLI with your package manager of choice. On macOS and Linux, the simplest route is the Homebrew tap, which handles updates for you. Windows users can download the signed installer from the releases page and run it with default options.

Once installed, run the version command to confirm the binary is on your path. If you see a not-found error, check that your shell profile includes the install directory, then open a new terminal window. Most issues at this step come from an old session that never picked up the change.

The first time you run the tool, it creates a config directory in your home folder. You can override that location with the CONFIG_HOME environment variable if you need to keep settings in a shared location.

Next, read the quickstart guide to create your first project.

Rotating an API key is one of those jobs everyone puts off, so here's the short version. First, generate a new key from the dashboard under Settings, then API Keys. Give it a name that says where it is used, like billing-worker-prod, so you remember what to update later.

Next, deploy the new key to the service that uses it. Don't delete the old one yet. Wait until you've confirmed traffic is flowing through the new key, which usually takes a few minutes if your logs are decent. You can check the last-used timestamp on each key in the same screen.

Once everything looks good, revoke the old key. It takes effect immediately, so do it during a quiet window if you can. If something breaks, you can re-issue the old key from the dashboard, though that creates a new value rather than restoring the original.

List endpoints in this API return results in pages, and the mechanism for moving between them is a cursor rather than a page number. Each response includes a next_cursor field when more results exist. Pass that value as the cursor query parameter on your next request to receive the following page.

Cursors are opaque strings. Do not try to decode them or build your own, because the format can change without notice. A cursor is tied to the sort order of the original request, so if you change the sort parameter partway through, you should start again from the first page.

When next_cursor is absent or null, you have reached the end of the collection. The limit parameter controls page size, with a default of 50 and a maximum of 200. Larger pages reduce request count but increase response time, so choose a size that fits your workload.

So webhooks fail sometimes. Your server is down for a deploy, the network hiccups, whatever. The good news is we retry, and you don't have to build your own queue for it.

Here's how it works. If your endpoint doesn't return a 2xx within ten seconds, we try again. The next attempts are spaced out, roughly one minute, five minutes, thirty minutes, and then a few hours, up to a total of about 24 hours. After that we give up and mark the delivery as failed.

You'll see every attempt in the delivery log, including the response code and body we got back. If you find a bug and want to replay something, there's a button for that. It resends the original payload with the same event ID, so make your handler idempotent. Check the event ID before you process anything twice.

To back up your Postgres database every night, you'll schedule a script with cron and keep the output in a dedicated directory. Start by creating the backup folder and making sure the user running the job has write access to it. A folder owned by root is the most common reason these jobs fail silently.

Next, write a short shell script that calls pg_dump with the custom format flag, then deletes dumps older than fourteen days. The custom format compresses the output and lets you restore selected tables later. Store the database password in a .pgpass file rather than in the script itself, and restrict its permissions to the owner.

Finally, add a cron entry that runs the script at 2 a.m. local time. Redirect both standard output and errors to a log file, so you can see what happened the morning after. Test the restore process once before you rely on the backups, because an untested backup is only a hope.

The rate limit headers tell you how close you are to being throttled, and most clients ignore them until they get a 429 back. Don't be that client. Every response includes X-RateLimit-Limit, which is the total number of requests allowed in the current window, and X-RateLimit-Remaining, which is how many you have left.

There's also X-RateLimit-Reset, a Unix timestamp for when the window resets. If you're running a batch job, this is the number to watch. When remaining gets low, sleep until the reset time instead of hammering the endpoint and getting cut off halfway through.

One thing that trips people up: the limits are per API key, not per IP address. If you run three workers on the same key, they share one budget. Split the keys if you need the throughput, and keep each one's usage in its own log so you can tell which worker is eating the quota.

Before any flag can be evaluated, the SDK must be initialized with your environment key and a user context. Create the client once when your application starts, and reuse it for the lifetime of the process. Creating a new client for every request is slow and unnecessary, because the client keeps a local cache of flag values.

The user context should include a stable identifier and any attributes you plan to target on, such as plan tier or region. Avoid putting personal data into attributes that are not needed for targeting. Once the client is ready, call the boolean evaluation method with the flag key and the user context, and provide a default value to return if the SDK cannot reach the service.

The default value matters more than most teams expect. Choose the safe option, usually the feature being off, so an outage never exposes unfinished functionality to every user.

Five years ago, I was convinced that the best product managers were the ones with the most ideas.

I was wrong.

The best product managers I have worked with are the ones who say no the most often, and who do it with clarity and empathy.

Here is what I have learned about saying no well:

1. Anchor every decision to the strategy. When a request does not align with this quarter's goals, say so explicitly. It depersonalizes the conversation.

2. Share the trade-off. Saying yes to this feature means saying no to something else. Make that visible.

3. Leave the door open. A no today is often a not yet. Capture the idea, explain when you will revisit it, and actually follow through.

4. Thank people for the input. Stakeholders who feel heard are far more likely to keep bringing you valuable insights.

Saying no is not about being difficult. It is about protecting your team's focus so they can deliver work that truly matters.

Cybersecurity is no longer just an IT problem. It is a business problem.

In the past year alone, we have seen ransomware attacks halt hospital operations, shut down manufacturing plants, and disrupt municipal services for weeks at a time. The financial cost is significant, but the reputational damage can be even harder to recover from.

Yet in many organizations, security is still treated as a line item rather than a strategic priority.

Here are three shifts I believe every leadership team should make:

First, bring security into the boardroom. Directors should understand your organization's top risks as clearly as they understand your revenue targets.

Second, invest in people, not just tools. Phishing remains the most common entry point for attackers, and regular, practical training is one of the most cost-effective defenses available.

Third, plan for when, not if. A tested incident response plan can turn a crisis into a manageable disruption.

The organizations that thrive will be the ones that treat resilience as a competitive advantage.

How is your organization approaching cybersecurity this year?

Last week, one of our junior engineers asked me a question that stopped me in my tracks: How do you know when you are ready for a senior role?

Authentication

All requests to the Fieldstone API must be authenticated using an API key. You can generate and manage API keys from the Developer Settings page in your Fieldstone dashboard.

Include your API key in the Authorization header of each request, using the Bearer scheme. For example, a request to list projects would include the header Authorization: Bearer fs_live_xxxxxxxx.

Fieldstone issues two types of keys. Test keys begin with fs_test_ and operate against a sandbox environment with sample data. Live keys begin with fs_live_ and access your production account. We recommend developing and testing your integration with a test key before switching to a live key.

API keys carry the same permissions as the user who created them. To limit access, create a dedicated service user with only the roles your integration requires.

Keep your keys secure. Do not commit them to source control or expose them in client-side code. If you believe a key has been compromised, revoke it immediately from the dashboard and generate a new one.

Requests made without a valid key will return a 401 Unauthorized response.

Getting Started

This guide walks you through installing Driftwood and running your first data pipeline locally.

Prerequisites: You will need Python 3.10 or later and Docker installed on your machine.

Step 1: Install the CLI. Run pip install driftwood-cli in your terminal. Once installation completes, verify it by running driftwood --version.

Step 2: Initialize a project. Navigate to an empty directory and run driftwood init. This creates a driftwood.yaml configuration file and a pipelines folder containing an example pipeline.

Step 3: Start the local runtime. Run driftwood up. This launches a lightweight scheduler and a local Postgres instance inside Docker. The first run may take a few minutes while images are downloaded.

Step 4: Run the example pipeline. Execute driftwood run example_pipeline. You should see log output as each task completes, followed by a summary showing the number of rows processed.

Step 5: View the results. Open http://localhost:8040 in your browser to explore the Driftwood UI, where you can inspect task history, logs, and data lineage.

Next steps: Learn how to connect your own data sources in the Connectors guide.

Rate Limits

To ensure reliable performance for all customers, the Parcelwise API enforces rate limits on a per-account basis.

By default, each account may make up to 100 requests per second and 50,000 requests per day. Bulk endpoints, such as batch label creation, count as a single request regardless of how many items are included, up to a maximum of 500 items per call.

Every response includes headers that describe your current usage. X-RateLimit-Limit indicates your maximum allowed requests in the current window, X-RateLimit-Remaining shows how many requests you have left, and X-RateLimit-Reset provides the time, in Unix epoch seconds, when the window resets.

If you exceed a limit, the API returns a 429 Too Many Requests response with a Retry-After header indicating how many seconds to wait before retrying. We recommend implementing exponential backoff with jitter to handle these responses gracefully.

If your use case requires higher limits, please contact our support team with details about your expected volume.

Troubleshooting: sync stuck at "waiting for device"

This one comes up a lot so writing it down.

Nine times out of ten it's the phone's battery optimization killing the background service. Android especially. Samsung is the worst offender, they have their own extra layer on top of the normal Android setting.

On a Samsung: Settings > Battery > Background usage limits > Never sleeping apps, add Tally. On other Android phones it's usually Settings > Apps > Tally > Battery > Unrestricted. Wording varies by manufacturer, sorry, there's no single path.

On iPhone make sure Background App Refresh is on for Tally. Also Low Power Mode turns it off silently which is annoying.

If you've done that and it's still stuck, force close the app on the phone, then hit Retry on the desktop. Don't hit retry a bunch of times in a row, it queues them and makes it worse (known bug, fix is in 3.8).

Still no luck? Grab the log from Help > Export diagnostics and send it to us.

## Why is my build slow?

Short answer: probably the image cache.

When you run `forge build` it checks the local cache for each layer first. If you've switched branches recently, or someone bumped the base image in `forge.toml`, most of the cache is invalid and it has to rebuild from scratch. First build after that will take 6-10 minutes on a normal laptop. After that it should be back to under a minute.

You can see what's being rebuilt with `forge build --explain`. Anything marked MISS is getting rebuilt.

A couple other things that have bitten people:

- Running inside a synced folder (Dropbox, iCloud Drive). The file watcher goes nuts. Move the repo somewhere else.
- Docker Desktop with less than 4GB memory. Builds don't fail, they just crawl. Check under Resources.
- Antivirus scanning node_modules on Windows. Exclude the project folder if your IT lets you.

If none of that helps, post the output of `forge doctor` in #build-help and someone will look.

Webhooks: how retries work

When something happens on your account (order paid, refund issued, etc) we POST a JSON body to the URL you gave us. We consider it delivered if your server responds with any 2xx within 10 seconds. Anything else, including a timeout, counts as a failure.

On failure we retry. The schedule is roughly 1 min, 5 min, 30 min, 2 hours, 6 hours, then every 12 hours until it's been 3 days. After that we give up and mark the event failed in the dashboard, you can resend it manually from there.

A few things worth knowing that people miss:

You will sometimes get the same event twice. Network stuff. Use the event_id field to dedupe, don't assume exactly-once.

Events can arrive out of order, especially during retries. If you care about ordering check the created_at timestamp rather than when it hit your server.

Respond fast. If you need to do something slow like send emails, put the event on a queue and return 200 right away. Most of the timeout failures we see are people doing all their work inside the request handler.

Setting up the label printer at the front counter

For new staff, or whoever's covering when Dana's out.

The printer is the white Zebra next to the register. It talks to the counter PC over USB, not wifi, so if it's unplugged nothing works and the error message won't tell you that.

1. Turn it on, the switch is on the back left. Wait for the light to go solid green. Blinking red means out of labels or the lid isn't clicked shut.
2. Labels go in with the shiny side up. Feed them under the little yellow guides, close the lid hard, it should spit out one blank label by itself. That's normal, it's calibrating.
3. In the POS go to Settings > Devices and make sure "ZD421 Counter" is picked, not "ZD421 Back". They look almost identical. The back one is the shipping printer.
4. Print a test. If it comes out but the text is shifted halfway off, hold the feed button for about 2 seconds till it blinks twice, then let go. Recalibrates.

If it's still being weird, text Dana, don't call the vendor, they charge us.
